question:
Patient note:
A 63-year-old woman with a long-standing history of chronic hepatitis C infection genotype 1b that was treated eight years ago with sofosbuvir/ledipasvir yet left her with residual stage 3 fibrosis, presented to the emergency department shortly after dawn complaining of “coal-black diarrhea” that had begun the previous afternoon and recurred three more times overnight, each episode described as thick and tar-like with a pungent odor that stained the toilet bowl and was difficult to flush clean. She added that the last movement occurred an hour before arrival and was accompanied by mild crampy epigastric discomfort but no nausea or vomiting. She specifically denied ever feeling faint, losing consciousness, seeing stars, or needing to brace herself when she stood up from bed during the night; she did note feeling more fatigued than usual and a bit light-headed when walking from the parking lot into triage. Apart from her hepatic condition she carries diagnoses of well-controlled hypothyroidism and osteoarthritis of the knees; she has never undergone variceal banding, never had documented ascites, and her most recent hepatology visit three months earlier reported stable laboratory indices and no sonographic evidence of portal vein thrombosis. Surgical history is limited to an open appendectomy in her twenties. Her medicines include levothyroxine 75 µg each morning, acetaminophen up to 3 g daily for joint pain, and a daily vitamin D supplement; she explicitly denies aspirin, non-steroidal anti-inflammatories, anticoagulants, or antiplatelet agents. She consumes one glass of wine on special occasions, quit cigarette smoking fifteen years ago after a 10-pack-year exposure, and has never used intravenous drugs since completing antiviral therapy. There is no family history of bleeding disorders or gastrointestinal malignancy. On arrival she was seated upright, conversant, and appeared pale but not diaphoretic. Initial vital signs obtained before any intravenous access or medications showed a blood pressure of 104/67 mm Hg in the left arm with an automated cuff, a regular heart rate of 91 beats per minute by pulse oximeter, respirations 18 per minute, oral temperature 36.8 °C, and oxygen saturation 98 % breathing ambient air. Capillary refill was brisk, jugular venous pulsation was not elevated, and peripheral pulses were symmetric. Sclerae were anicteric, though conjunctival pallor was noted; oral mucosa was moist without telangiectasias. The chest was clear to auscultation bilaterally, and cardiac examination revealed normal S1 and S2 without gallops, rubs, or murmurs. Abdominal inspection showed no distention; on palpation the abdomen was soft with mild tenderness localized to the epigastrium and right upper quadrant, without guarding, rebound, or palpable masses. No shifting dullness or fluid wave was appreciated, and the liver edge was not palpable below the costal margin. Several spider angiomas were visible over the upper chest, consistent with her known hepatic background. Bowel sounds were hyperactive. A digital rectal examination produced a generous smear of pitch-black, glossy stool that turned the bedside guaiac card deep blue within seconds. Neurologic screening demonstrated an alert, oriented individual with intact cranial nerves and full motor strength in all extremities; gait was not assessed in view of active bleeding concerns. Two 16-gauge peripheral intravenous catheters were placed after phlebotomy, but no crystalloids, blood products, vasoactive agents, proton pump inhibitors, or antibiotics had yet been administered. Laboratory studies drawn at triage revealed hemoglobin 11.7 g/dL, hematocrit 34 %, mean corpuscular volume 89 fL, platelet count 192 × 10⁹/L, white blood cell count 7.3 × 10⁹/L, blood urea nitrogen 33 mg/dL, serum creatinine 1.0 mg/dL (baseline 0.9 mg/dL), sodium 137 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, chloride 104 mmol/L, bicarbonate 23 mmol/L, and glucose 108 mg/dL. Liver panel returned alanine aminotransferase 52 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 49 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 112 U/L, total bilirubin 1.1 mg/dL, albumin 3.4 g/dL, and an international normalized ratio of 1.3, similar to her outpatient baseline. Electrocardiography performed moments after arrival demonstrated normal sinus rhythm at 90–92 bpm without acute ischemic changes. Upright chest radiography showed clear lung fields and an unremarkable mediastinum; an abdominal radiograph revealed a nonspecific gas pattern without evidence of perforation. A type and crossmatch for two units of packed red blood cells was sent, the patient was kept nil per os, and gastroenterology was contacted for urgent esophagogastroduodenoscopy once hemodynamic stability was confirmed.

Question: What is the patient's Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding score? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding Score uses admission BUN, sex-specific hemoglobin, systolic pressure, pulse, melena, syncope, hepatic disease, and cardiac failure.
• BUN 33 mg/dL corresponds to urea about 11.8 mmol/L (10 to <25): +4.
• Hemoglobin 11.7 g/dL in a woman (10 to <12): +1.
• Systolic pressure 104 mm Hg (100–109): +1.
• Pulse 91/min (<100): 0.
• Melena confirmed by tarry black stool: +1.
• Syncope: 0. She felt light-headed but did not lose consciousness.
• Hepatic disease: +2 for residual stage 3 fibrosis after hepatitis C treatment.
• Cardiac failure: none documented, 0.
Total = 4 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 0 + 2 + 0 = 9.
Final answer: 9
